subsection: 7. Republican and Loyalist terrorism and the Republic's responses to the Troubles, 1969–1993

notes.h: Terms and background: terrorism, sectarianism, propaganda and the two communities
notes.b: Three ideas run through the whole story of violence in the Troubles, and they rest on the divide between Northern Ireland's two communities. Knowing the terms makes it easier to judge each attack and each response.
points: Northern Ireland had two main communities: unionists or loyalists, mostly Protestant, who wanted to stay in the United Kingdom, and nationalists or republicans, mostly Catholic, who wanted a united Ireland. Loyalists are unionists who accept violence, and republicans seek a united Ireland.

Terrorism means violence against civilians and the state for political aims. Both republican and loyalist groups used it, which is why bombings and shootings are judged as political acts and not only as crimes.

Sectarianism means hostility and violence between Protestants and Catholics, based on religious identity and political allegiance. It explains why so many victims were ordinary civilians killed only because of their community.

Propaganda means murals, publications, broadcasts and statements used to win opinion, and also the broadcast bans that tried to deny paramilitaries a voice. Each side needed public support, so the fight for opinion ran alongside the fighting.
The Troubles began in 1968 to 1969, and the British army was deployed in August 1969. Direct Rule, meaning government of Northern Ireland straight from London, came in March 1972.
notes.tip: Define terrorism, sectarianism and propaganda in your own words when they appear in an answer, and tie each to a named example, because a definition with no example earns little.

notes.h: The Provisional IRA: origins, aims and methods
notes.b: The Provisional IRA was the biggest republican paramilitary group and the one that killed the most people in the Troubles. It came out of a split in the older IRA and set itself the aim of ending British rule by force.
points: The IRA split in December 1969 into the Provisional IRA, led by Seán Mac Stíofáin, and the Official IRA, led by Cathal Goulding. The Provisionals rejected the Officials' policy and took up armed defence of Catholic areas, and then a campaign against British rule.

The Provisionals' aims were to end British rule in Northern Ireland and to bring about a united Ireland through a campaign of armed attacks, because they believed only force would make Britain withdraw.

Their targets were British soldiers, members of the RUC (the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's police) and the UDR (the Ulster Defence Regiment, a locally recruited army regiment), and also civilians.
Their methods were bombings, shootings and car bombs. Car bombs were used because a vehicle could carry a large charge into a town centre or onto a street with little warning.
The Provisional IRA was responsible for the largest number of killings in the Troubles, followed by the loyalists of the UDA and UVF, so it dominates any account of who caused the deaths.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on the Provisional IRA, give the aims (end British rule, a united Ireland), the split of December 1969, Seán Mac Stíofáin, and three or four dated attacks such as Bloody Friday, Birmingham and Enniskillen.

notes.h: Provisional IRA attacks in Northern Ireland and on the Irish border
notes.b: The Provisional IRA's campaign in Northern Ireland hit soldiers, police, civilians and, in some attacks, Protestant communities. Several of the worst attacks also caused public revulsion, which damaged republican claims to be defending their community.
points: Bloody Friday, 21 July 1972, saw more than twenty bombs go off in Belfast in about an hour and a half, killing nine people. The bombs were spread across the city so that police and the public could not cope with all the warnings.
On 27 August 1979 Lord Mountbatten was killed with three others, one of them a fourteen-year-old grandson, by a bomb on his boat at Mullaghmore, County Sligo.
On the same day eighteen British soldiers were killed in two bombs at Warrenpoint, County Down. Mullaghmore and Warrenpoint were separate attacks, so keep them apart in an answer.

The Enniskillen bombing, 8 November 1987, killed eleven people at a Remembrance Day ceremony. Gordon Wilson, whose daughter Marie died, publicly forgave the bombers, and this made the attack even more shocking.

Attacks on Protestants included the La Mon House Hotel firebomb near Belfast in February 1978, which killed twelve people, and Teebane, County Tyrone, in January 1992, where eight Protestant workmen were killed.

At Kingsmill, South Armagh, in January 1976, ten Protestant workmen were shot dead. The killings were attributed to republicans, were claimed under a cover name, and followed the killing of Catholics by loyalists.

The Shankill Road fish shop bomb of 23 October 1993 killed ten people, including one of the two bombers. The target was thought to be a loyalist meeting upstairs, but the dead were people in the shop.
notes.tip: Keep similar attacks apart: Mountbatten was killed at Mullaghmore and Warrenpoint was the same day's different attack. Date each attack, because correct dated statements are what earn the marks.

notes.b: From 1974 the IRA took its campaign to England, bombing pubs, London parks, a department store and a party conference. These attacks aimed to put pressure on the British public and government, and two of them led to wrongful convictions.
points: The Guildford pub bombings of 5 October 1974 killed five people. The Guildford Four, convicted of them, were freed in 1989 when their convictions were overturned.

The Birmingham pub bombings of 21 November 1974 killed 21 people. The IRA never formally claimed them, and the Birmingham Six, convicted of them, were freed in 1991 when their convictions were quashed.
The IRA bombed Hyde Park and Regent's Park in London on 20 July 1982, killing eleven soldiers and bandsmen, who were chosen as military targets in public places.
A bomb at Harrods in December 1983 killed six people, and it showed that civilian shoppers in central London could be caught up in the campaign.
The Brighton bombing of 12 October 1984 killed five people. It was aimed at the Conservative government at its party conference, and Margaret Thatcher survived.
The Warrington bombing of 20 March 1993 killed two boys, Johnathan Ball, aged 3, and Tim Parry, aged 12, and injured many more. Warrington was an IRA bomb, not a loyalist one.
notes.tip: Guildford (October 1974) and Birmingham (November 1974) are easy to swap, as are Brighton (1984) and Warrington (1993). Give the date with each, and mention that the Guildford Four and Birmingham Six convictions were overturned.

notes.h: The INLA, arms supply and Irish-American funding
notes.b: The Provisional IRA was not the only republican group, and it needed weapons and money to keep going. Arms from abroad and funds from the United States kept the campaign supplied.
points: The Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) was a republican splinter group of the mid-1970s, separate from both the Provisional and Official IRA.
The INLA killed 17 people in the Droppin' Well bar bombing at Ballykelly, County Londonderry, in December 1982. 11 of the dead were soldiers, because the bar was popular with the army.
A cargo of arms from Libya on the ship Eksund was seized by French customs in November 1987, which showed how the IRA was supplied for its campaign from abroad.
NORAID, an Irish-American fundraising committee formed in 1970, gave republicans funds and publicity in the United States.
notes.tip: Keep the groups separate: Provisional IRA, Official IRA and INLA are different organisations, and Ballykelly was an INLA attack, not a Provisional IRA one.

notes.h: Loyalist paramilitaries: UVF, UDA and UFF
notes.b: Loyalist paramilitaries rose to defend the Union and to oppose a united Ireland and power sharing, meaning the sharing of government between unionists and nationalists. In practice most of their victims were Catholic civilians.
points: The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) was revived in 1966 and carried out attacks in the early years of the Troubles, including bombings and shootings.

The Ulster Defence Association (UDA) was formed in 1971 as an umbrella for local loyalist groups. The Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF), formed in 1973, was the UDA's cover name for killings, so the UDA could deny them.
Their aims were to defend the Union with Britain, and to oppose a united Ireland and power sharing, because they feared Catholic and nationalist influence in government.
Loyalist paramilitaries claimed to be defending the Union, but most of their victims were Catholic civilians with no paramilitary links. This is why their violence is described as sectarian.
UVF and UDA gunmen attacked Catholic bars and homes in Belfast during the 1970s, and Catholic workers on the roads, because any Catholic could be chosen as a target.
notes.tip: For Ordinary Level, name the UVF, UDA and UFF, say what they aimed at, and give one or two attacks with the year. Remember the UFF was the UDA's cover name, not a separate group.

notes.h: Loyalist attacks: McGurk's Bar to Greysteel
notes.b: Loyalist attacks hit Catholic civilians in bars, in a Dublin street and on a country road. They became more frequent again in the early 1990s, when loyalists answered republican attacks with attacks on Catholic crowds.
points: The bombing of McGurk's Bar in Belfast on 4 December 1971 killed 15 Catholic civilians, so the attack was sectarian. Police first blamed the IRA, but the Police Ombudsman reported in 2011 that the UVF was responsible.
On 17 May 1974 car bombs in Dublin and Monaghan killed 33 people and an unborn child. This was the largest loss of life in a single day of the Troubles, and the attack was attributed to the UVF.
The Miami Showband killings of 31 July 1975 saw UVF men kill three members of a popular band at a fake army checkpoint in County Down, a disguise that made the victims stop and trust the men.
On 5 February 1992 the UFF killed five Catholics at Sean Graham's bookmakers on the Ormeau Road, Belfast. Loyalist killing rose sharply in the early 1990s.

The Greysteel massacre of 30 October 1993 saw the UFF kill eight people at the Rising Sun bar, at a Halloween dance. It came a week after the Shankill bomb, and was the UFF's response to it, not an IRA reprisal.
notes.tip: McGurk's Bar (UVF, Belfast, 1971) and the Dublin and Monaghan bombings (UVF, 1974) are often confused, so give the place and year for each. For Greysteel, say it was loyalist retaliation for the Shankill bomb.

notes.b: Some loyalist groups carried out sectarian murders of Catholics that were marked by torture and brutality, and the Shankill Butchers were the most notorious. Their crimes shocked people in both communities.
points: The Shankill Butchers were a UVF gang from the Shankill Road in west Belfast, who abducted Catholics at night and killed them between 1975 and 1977.
Many victims were killed with knives and hatchets, which led to widespread revulsion in both communities because the killings were so cruel.
The gang was led by Lenny Murphy, and eleven members were convicted in 1979 of a series of murders, receiving many life sentences.
The gang's activities showed how sectarian violence could develop outside the formal paramilitary chains of command, and Murphy himself was shot dead in 1982.
notes.tip: The Shankill bomb (an IRA attack in 1993) and the Shankill Butchers (a UVF gang, 1975 to 1977) are different events. Name the group and the dates every time.

notes.b: Counting the dead shows how widely responsibility for killing was spread. It also shows that most of the violence came from paramilitaries and not the state.
points: About 3,500 people were killed between 1969 and 2001, about 3,000 of them by 1993. About half of the dead were civilians.
Republican paramilitaries were responsible for about 60 per cent of the deaths, loyalist paramilitaries for about 30 per cent and the security forces for about 10 per cent.
The worst year was 1972, with nearly 500 deaths, and the number of deaths fell sharply in the 1980s.
Loyalist killing rose sharply in the early 1990s, with many attacks on Catholics, so loyalist groups became a larger share of the violence late in the period.
notes.tip: Give casualty figures as about, and attribute them to the three groups of republicans, loyalists and the security forces. Do not give false precision, and say the Provisional IRA killed the most.

notes.h: Security force operations and republican losses
notes.b: The army and RUC fought the IRA with searches, arrests and surveillance, and with some armed ambushes. Several incidents led to allegations that the security forces had used lethal force unlawfully.
points: The British army and RUC carried out searches, arrests and surveillance operations that disrupted IRA units, but the IRA continued to recruit and attack, so security pressure alone did not end the campaign.
Republicans argued that the army's arrests and searches in Catholic areas increased recruitment to the IRA, because they alienated people who might otherwise have stayed out of the conflict.
At Loughgall, County Armagh, on 8 May 1987, the SAS (the army's special forces) killed eight IRA men attacking an RUC station. A civilian who happened to drive by was also killed.
The Gibraltar shootings of 6 March 1988 saw the SAS kill three unarmed IRA members, Mairéad Farrell, Daniel McCann and Seán Savage, and they raised questions about the use of lethal force.

Loughgall and Gibraltar fed an allegation of a 'shoot to kill' policy, meaning that suspects were killed instead of arrested. It was an allegation, and the incidents are not proof of an official policy.
The Stalker inquiry, from 1984, and the Sampson inquiry followed RUC shootings of unarmed men in 1982, and they added to the 'shoot to kill' controversy.
notes.tip: When writing about Loughgall and Gibraltar, say that 'shoot to kill' was alleged and not proven, and give the republican view that security operations fed recruitment.

notes.h: Propaganda and the battle for public opinion
notes.b: Both republicans and loyalists used murals, publications and political statements to shape public opinion. The British and Irish governments responded by trying to deny the paramilitaries publicity on air.
points: Republican murals celebrated IRA volunteers, so they became a central feature of the political landscape, and loyalist murals in Protestant areas celebrated the UVF and UDA and presented their violence as a defence of loyal communities.
Republicans used publications such as An Phoblacht to present their case, and their propaganda stressed the British occupation.
Irish-American support for republicans provided funds and publicity for the republican campaign, so the cause was heard beyond Ireland.

In October 1988 the British government banned the broadcast of the voices of spokesmen for eleven organisations, including Sinn Féin, the IRA and loyalist groups. Broadcasters used actors' voices, and the ban was lifted in 1994.
The British ban was intended to deny publicity to terrorist groups, but critics said it restricted freedom of expression, and the use of actors showed how easy it was to get round.

In the Republic, Section 31 of the Broadcasting Authority Act 1960 was used through ministerial orders that barred broadcast interviews with the IRA and later Sinn Féin. It was allowed to lapse in 1994, the same year as the British ban.
notes.tip: Do not mix up Section 31 (the Republic's ban on broadcast interviews) and the British voice ban of 1988. Give the reason for each ban and a view of how effective it was.

notes.b: The Republic's government (the Taoiseach is its prime minister) answered the violence of August 1969 with words, aid and a border presence. The Arms Crisis of 1970 then split the governing party, Fianna Fáil, and Bloody Sunday brought an angry public reaction.
points: On 13 August 1969 the Taoiseach Jack Lynch broadcast that the government 'can no longer stand by' while Catholics were attacked in Belfast and Derry, and he asked for a United Nations peacekeeping force.
The Irish army set up field hospitals near the border. Refugees from Belfast and Derry were housed in army camps such as Gormanston, County Meath.

In May 1970 Lynch dismissed Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney on 6 May, after allegations that money for relief was being used to import arms for Northern nationalists. This was the Arms Crisis, and it divided Fianna Fáil.
At the Arms Trial in autumn 1970, Haughey, Captain James Kelly, John Kelly and Albert Luykx were tried for conspiracy to import arms. They were acquitted in October 1970.
After Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, when 13 were killed in Derry, the Irish government declared a day of mourning and recalled its ambassador from London for consultations.
The British embassy in Merrion Square, Dublin, was burned on 2 February 1972 during a demonstration, as anger over Bloody Sunday boiled over.
notes.tip: Learn the sequence Lynch's broadcast (1969), the Arms Crisis (1970), embassy burning (1972), with one result for each. Keep the Arms Crisis (the dismissals) separate from the Arms Trial (the acquittals).

notes.h: The Republic's security laws and the Cosgrave government, 1972–1976
notes.b: As the Northern conflict spread south, the Republic tightened its laws against the IRA. The coalition of Liam Cosgrave also backed the Sunningdale settlement, to show Dublin's support for cross-border cooperation.
points: The IRA was declared an unlawful organisation in 1936, and the Offences against the State Act 1939 created the Special Criminal Court, which has no jury and three judges, so verdicts could not be swayed by juror intimidation.
The Special Criminal Court was revived in 1972 to try paramilitary offences, because juries could be intimidated.

The Offences against the State (Amendment) Act 1972 was passed in December 1972, after loyalist car bombs in Dublin. It allowed a chief superintendent's statement that he believed a person to be an IRA member to be accepted as evidence.

Cosgrave's Fine Gael and Labour coalition, in power from 1973 to 1977, signed the Sunningdale Agreement in December 1973, which included a Council of Ireland. Garda (Irish police) cooperation with the RUC increased, because both forces faced the same IRA threat.
The Criminal Law (Jurisdiction) Act 1976 allowed certain offences committed in Northern Ireland to be tried in the Republic, so suspects who fled south could still face a court.
The IRA killed the British ambassador, Christopher Ewart-Biggs, in July 1976, and the Emergency Powers Act 1976 followed, giving the state stronger powers in response.
President Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh referred the Emergency Powers bill to the Supreme Court. He resigned in October 1976 after a government minister criticised him.
notes.tip: Keep the Offences against the State Act 1939 and its 1972 Amendment Act apart. Say why each was needed, and link every response in the Republic to a crisis in the North.

notes.h: The Republic, extradition and the Anglo-Irish process, 1980s
notes.b: In the 1980s the Republic's governments worked with Britain on a political settlement while extradition, the handing over of wanted people to another state, stayed a source of tension.
points: Charles Haughey, Taoiseach in 1979 to 1981, 1982 and 1987 to 1992, held a summit with Margaret Thatcher in Dublin in December 1980 to study 'the totality of relationships' between the two islands.

Garret FitzGerald, Taoiseach in 1981 to 1982 and 1982 to 1987, pursued the New Ireland Forum of 1983 to 1984. He signed the Anglo-Irish Agreement with Thatcher at Hillsborough on 15 November 1985, which set up an Intergovernmental Conference.
Unionists complained that the Republic gained too much influence through the Intergovernmental Conference. The Agreement also put cross-border security cooperation on a formal footing.
Fianna Fáil under Haughey voted against the Agreement in 1985, but kept it in place when it returned to power in 1987.

Extradition was a recurring dispute between Dublin and London. The Extradition (European Convention on the Suppression of Terrorism) Act 1987 was passed in December 1987, after the Enniskillen bombing.
notes.tip: Answers on the Republic's response should link each step to events in the North, for example the 1987 Extradition Act to Enniskillen. A list with no links earns little.

notes.b: Judging terrorism means weighing what it did against what it set out to achieve. The best answers state a view, pairing impact with failure and contemporary opinion with later judgement.
points: Impact: terrorism killed large numbers of civilians and security force members, and it made political compromise harder by hardening attitudes on all sides.
Impact: republican and loyalist campaigns shaped British and Irish policy, because security measures and political initiatives were both shaped by the need to contain violence.

Failure: neither the IRA nor the loyalist groups achieved their stated aims, a united Ireland or the defence of the Union, and the main IRA and loyalist ceasefires came in 1994, after the period covered here.
Failure: terrorism deepened sectarian divisions, and its victims in both communities created lasting grievances.
Contemporary view: the British and Irish governments condemned terrorism and sought to isolate paramilitaries from political influence.
Contemporary view: republicans argued that the IRA was defending the Catholic community and fighting an occupying power, while loyalists claimed to defend the Union.
Later view: historians point out that most of the killing was done by paramilitary groups, not the state, and that the long campaign persuaded many in each group that violence could not win.

Later view: the Republic's responses leaned on security measures, such as the Special Criminal Court and extradition, while its political aims were pursued through Sunningdale and the Anglo-Irish Agreement.
notes.tip: A high-marks essay needs a clear thesis, both republican and loyalist violence, named attacks with dates, and a judgement of impact against failure to achieve aims. Description without judgement scores poorly.

keyTerms.definition: The use of violence against civilians and the state to achieve political aims, which both republican and loyalist paramilitaries used between 1969 and 1993.
Hostility and violence between Protestants and Catholics based on religious identity and political allegiance, shown most clearly in loyalist sectarian murders.
The use of murals, publications, broadcasts and statements to shape public opinion, and in the 1988 case the restriction of broadcast voices.

The republican paramilitary organisation formed in December 1969 that carried out the main armed campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland, responsible for the largest number of Troubles deaths.
The loyalist paramilitary organisation revived in 1966, responsible for many attacks on Catholic civilians including the 1974 Dublin and Monaghan bombings.
The May 1970 affair in which ministers in the Irish government were accused of approving arms imports for Northern nationalists, leading to the dismissal of Charles Haughey and Neil Blaney.
A court in the Republic, re-established in 1972, that tried offences linked to paramilitary violence without a jury.
The contested allegation that British security forces deliberately killed suspects rather than arresting them, which became an issue after incidents such as Loughgall in 1987.
The provision in Irish broadcasting law that barred broadcasters from interviewing spokesmen for the IRA and later Sinn Féin, allowed to lapse in 1994.
The cover name used by the UDA for sectarian killings from 1973.
A republican paramilitary group formed in 1975, responsible for the Ballykelly bombing of 1982.
